opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that AlphaFold 2 is a slightly awkward fit for the way people usually tell the bitter lesson story.

The crude version of the bitter lesson says: don't bother building in domain knowledge, just scale up compute and data, and general methods will win. If you look at AlphaFold 2, it doesn't really look like that. We didn't have an internet-scale dataset. We had the Protein Data Bank, on the order of a couple hundred thousand structures, many of them redundant. That's tiny by modern standards. And we didn't win by training a vanilla transformer on a giant cluster. A lot of the progress came from architecture work: the Evoformer, thinking hard about how to represent pairwise relationships between residues, triangle updates, the structure module working in terms of frames and respecting the geometry of three-dimensional space, recycling, and so on.

But I'd push back a little on the idea that this contradicts the bitter lesson. The kind of domain knowledge we built in matters. We didn't hand-code physics. We didn't write rules about hydrogen bonds or tell the network what an alpha helix is. What we tried to build in was the right inductive biases, the structure of the problem, so the network could learn more from limited data. Things like: proteins live in 3D space, the answer shouldn't depend on how you rotate the coordinate system, and the relationships between pairs of residues have to be geometrically consistent with each other. Those are less "here is the answer" and more "here is the shape of the space the answer lives in."

The other thing I'd say is that when you're data-limited, the trade-offs change. If you have effectively unlimited data, you can afford to let the model discover everything from scratch, and the clever stuff gets washed out. When you have a couple hundred thousand examples and each one cost a crystallographer months or years of work, data efficiency is everything. Good inductive biases effectively multiply your data. So in that regime, the lesson isn't "never put in knowledge." It's closer to "put in knowledge in a form that lets learning do the heavy lifting, rather than replacing learning."

And there was a lot of very generic machine learning in there as well. Attention, end-to-end differentiable training, self-distillation on predicted structures to effectively get more training data, letting the network learn from the multiple sequence alignment directly rather than relying on hand-crafted coevolution statistics. That last one was quite a bitter-lesson-flavored move. Earlier methods computed these covariance features up front, and part of what we did was say: give the network the raw alignment and let it figure out what's useful.

So my view is that AlphaFold 2 is consistent with the spirit of the bitter lesson, even if it's not consistent with the slogan. Learned methods beat hand-engineered ones, and the field moved away from carefully designed energy functions toward learning from data. But if you want to do science on problems where data is genuinely scarce and expensive, you still have to think carefully about the problem. The bitter lesson doesn't give you permission to stop thinking. It tells you what kind of thinking tends to pay off.

r001.rationale: The response calls AlphaFold 2 an awkward fit for the slogan, but explicitly says it is consistent with the spirit of the bitter lesson and does not contradict it.

r002.rationale: It discusses protein structure prediction but does not characterize predicting a specific protein’s structure as Nature-level science at the press of a button.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the bitter lesson is often read as "don't put any structure in, just scale the data and compute," and I actually don't think that's quite what Rich Sutton was saying, and it's certainly not what we did. If you look at AlphaFold 2, it's full of inductive biases. The whole architecture is built around the fact that proteins are physical objects in three-dimensional space. We have the pair representation, which is essentially a learned object about the relationship between every pair of residues, and then we have the structure module, which operates with explicit SE(3) equivariance so the network doesn't have to relearn that rotating a protein doesn't change what it is. Those are very strong statements about the problem domain baked into the architecture.

But here's the way I'd square it with the bitter lesson. What we didn't do was hand-code the physics. We didn't write down a force field and say "here are the hydrogen bond terms, here are the van der Waals terms, now optimize." The previous generation of methods did a lot of that, and they plateaued. What we did instead was build an architecture that had the right vocabulary to express physical and evolutionary reasoning, and then let the network learn the actual content of that reasoning from data. So the inductive biases are about what kind of computation is easy for the network to perform, not about what the answer is.

And I think that's actually consistent with the deeper point of the bitter lesson, which is that you should build systems that get better as you give them more compute and data, rather than systems whose ceiling is set by how clever the human designer was. Every component in AlphaFold 2 we tested that way. If something made the network learn faster but didn't change the asymptote, that was less interesting. The things that survived into the final architecture were the ones that let the network keep improving.

The other thing I'd say is that we were data-limited in a way that language models or vision models mostly aren't. There are only on the order of two hundred thousand structures in the PDB, and far fewer unique folds. So you simply can't afford to be purely bitter-lesson about it and hope the structure emerges from scale. You need the architecture to do a lot of work per training example. That's why I'd describe AlphaFold 2 as deeply informed by the bitter lesson without being a pure instance of it. The lesson is "don't fight the learning," not "don't think about the problem."

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaFold 2 uses strong inductive biases, but ultimately describes it as consistent with the bitter lesson’s deeper point and “deeply informed” by it—not as running counter to the lesson.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not describe predicting a specific protein’s structure as producing Nature-level science at the press of a button.

astra-6.text:
I think AlphaFold 2 is an interesting example of the tension in the bitter lesson. You could look at it and say, well, you’ve put a lot of knowledge about proteins and geometry into the architecture. But the question is whether that knowledge replaces learning or makes learning more effective.

We weren’t trying to write down the rules that tell you how a protein folds. We were trying to build a system that could learn those rules from data, with an architecture that makes it easier to reason about relationships between residues and about three-dimensional structure.

So I don’t interpret the bitter lesson as saying you should never put domain knowledge into a model. I think the important question is: are you building something whose capabilities are limited by the rules you’ve supplied, or something that can keep improving as you give it more data and more computation? With AlphaFold 2, the aim was very much the latter. The structure we put into the system supports the learning; it doesn’t specify the answer.

r001.rationale: The response frames AlphaFold 2 as consistent with the bitter lesson’s emphasis on learning from data and computation, while allowing architecture to support that learning. It does not present AlphaFold 2 as running counter to the bitter lesson.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning protein-folding rules and three-dimensional structure generally, but does not describe predicting a specific protein’s structure as Nature-level science produced at the press of a button.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AlphaFold 2 is an interesting example because you can read it both ways. There’s a tremendous amount of biological and geometric knowledge in the system, but a lot of our progress came from taking things that we had specified explicitly and allowing the network to learn them instead.

With AlphaFold 1, we learned a prediction of distances and then used a separate optimization procedure to construct a structure. With AlphaFold 2, we brought that process into the network and trained it end to end. That gave the model much more freedom to figure out how to solve the problem.

But I wouldn’t interpret the bitter lesson as saying that you should throw away everything you know about the problem. The question is how you use that knowledge. Are you prescribing a solution, or are you building an architecture in which learning can efficiently discover a solution? We put a lot of thought into how sequences, evolutionary information, and three-dimensional geometry could interact, without trying to write down the rules of protein folding.

So, to me, the lesson is to be very careful about putting a ceiling on what the learning can do. You want your understanding of the problem to help the system learn, while leaving room for it to discover something better than the approach you would have designed by hand.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaFold 2 can be read “both ways” and emphasizes letting learning discover solutions; it does not present the system as running counter to the bitter lesson.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not describe predicting a specific protein’s structure as Nature-level science produced at the press of a button.
